description:
In 1817, New York began digging a canal across its wild western frontier, from Albany on the Hudson River to Buffalo on Lake Erie. Critics called it Clinton's Ditch. Eight years later it was the most talked about engineering feat in America.

This documentary tells the story of the Erie Canal, the 363 mile waterway championed by Governor DeWitt Clinton. We follow the crews who dug it largely by hand and with animal power, the 83 locks that lifted boats over the land, and the aqueducts that carried the canal across rivers. We see the opening in October 1825, when Clinton poured a keg of Lake Erie water into New York Harbor in a ceremony called the Wedding of the Waters.

The canal cost about 7 million dollars and cut the cost of shipping freight from the Great Lakes to New York by about 90 percent. Tolls soon paid back the debt, towns boomed along its path, and New York City became the leading port in the nation. Mules on the towpath pulled the boats, and the songs they inspired are still sung today.

Figures are drawn from widely published histories of the canal; costs and savings are approximate.
